name: Aisha Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing nursing at a city university about forty minutes by train from home. I share a flat with two girls from my course, and most weeks are lectures Monday to Wednesday, a skills lab on Thursday where we practise on dummies, and a Saturday shift at a bakery I kept from school. I handwrite all my notes, because I remember things better that way. Honestly the lab days are my favourite, and the anatomy reading is what wears me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine and that hospitals have run on people for a hundred years. Some software for rotas or booking is no problem. I'd tell my flatmates the hype was always louder than the truth, and I'd probably post nothing, because I don't like arguing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel relieved, but I also know the NHS-style funding squeeze doesn't care about AI. Wards are short of staff either way. Nobody ever had a wound dressed by a hype cycle, so I'm not worried about the robots part at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. I'd keep the Saturday shift at the bakery, keep handwriting notes, and join the student nurses' branch of the union in the spring like my mum's friend told me to. I'd save my allowance for a placement-year car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit tired when I think about how stretched wards already are, but that isn't new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the squeeze worries you more than AI. Who do you blame for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments, honestly, for years of cuts, and the big companies that pay almost no tax. Mum says the hospital she cleans at has had the same number of porters since before I was born, with twice the patients. If AI saves them money, I want that money kept on the wards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a lecturer started requiring AI tools in your course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it for the marks but I'd hate it. I'd ask what happens to patient data first, because nobody has ever explained that clearly to me.

say: Hospitals have run on **people** for a hundred years and will keep doing so.
I'd post nothing online because I don't like arguing.
think: The real danger is the **funding squeeze**, not AI, and it hits wards either way.
I'm relieved that hands-on care looks safe.
do: Keep the **Saturday bakery shift** and handwritten notes.
Join the student nurses' **union branch** in spring.
Save allowance toward a **car** for placement year.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a tired edge about stretched wards.
S0.quote: Nobody ever had a wound dressed by a hype cycle, so I'm not worried about the robots part at all.
fieldNote: She blames **cuts** and low corporate tax, not the technology.
Her calm is based on hands-on care feeling untouchable.
She would comply with AI tools for marks but resents it.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday bakery shift and the handwritten notes
Join the student nurses' union branch in the spring
Put part of the monthly allowance aside for a placement car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a worry for office jobs but not for the bedside. I'd tell my course group that nurses need to be at the table when hospitals decide what software to buy. I'd also say any AI that writes patient notes must be checked by a human, every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm safer than most, but I'm not sure my degree stays as respected if AI takes over the reading and charting parts. Mum's school office is already using software to write letters to parents, and her colleague wasn't replaced when she left. That's the sort of thing I'd see more of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on my course and push the union branch to ask for training that's paid for by the hospital, not by us. I'd learn what the new systems do, but only the ones on placement, because I don't want to chase tools. I'd also keep my savings untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Things around me are shifting and I don't feel in control of who decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at university would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Dalia on the business course. Her lecturers keep saying entry-level analyst jobs are what AI does first. She's laughing about it, but she's been quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this make you want to change course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I picked nursing because I like people, and Steady Disruption doesn't change that. If anything I'd feel more sure about it.

say: Nurses must be **at the table** when hospitals choose software.
Anything AI writes in patient notes must be **checked by a human**.
think: My job feels safer than **office work**, but charting tasks could move to software.
Mum's school office already **didn't replace** a leaver.
do: Stay on the course and ask the union branch for **hospital-paid training**.
Learn only the systems used on **placement**.
feel: **Uneasy**, because others will decide how these tools arrive.
S1.quote: I picked nursing because I like people, and Steady Disruption doesn't change that. If anything I'd feel more sure about it.
fieldNote: Her worry is about **who decides**, not about losing her job.
She links the picture to **her mum's** school office.
She stays loyal to her course choice.

steps.text: Stay on the nursing course and keep the placement plans
Ask the union branch to demand hospital-paid software training
Learn the charting system used on first placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is moving far too fast and it's the governments' job to slow it down. I'd sign any petition and go to a union rally if one was organised in our city. I'd tell my friends that nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm frightened. Two years is when I'd be finishing my second year, and I'd have no idea what the hospital will look like. I keep thinking the thinking jobs go first and then budgets collapse around us, and the ward gets cut even if the robots aren't ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay and finish the course, because I wouldn't know what else to do. I'd talk to my mum about whether I should work extra shifts now to build a cushion. I'd go to every union meeting and write to our local politician about training and funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I feel like everything I've planned is on a clock somebody else is holding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. With ten years I could take my time, but with two I won't even have qualified before the thinking work goes. I'd want a promise from the government that nursing jobs will be protected, and I'd hate that I'm relying on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not quitting, and I'd ask if we could keep the family's spare money in savings, not spent on my fees early. That's an odd thing to say, but I'd feel safer.

say: This is moving **too fast** and governments must slow it down.
I'd sign **petitions** and attend a union rally.
think: I'm **frightened**, because I'd barely be qualified before the thinking work goes.
Budgets could collapse even if **robots** aren't ready.
do: Finish the course and work **extra shifts** at the bakery for a cushion.
Attend every **union meeting** and write to our local politician.
feel: **Anxious**, as if the plan is on a clock held by someone else.
S2.quote: I'd say I'm not quitting, and I'd ask if we could keep the family's spare money in savings, not spent on my fees early.
fieldNote: The **two-year clock** is what moves her from uneasy to anxious.
She turns to **collective action** because she doesn't trust individual fixes.
She frames her fear as a funding risk, not a robot risk.

steps.text: Pick up extra bakery shifts to build a cushion
Go to every student nurses' union meeting this year
Write to the local politician about nurse funding and training
Finish the second-year nursing exams without changing course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still scary but at least we'd have some warning. I'd tell my friends we should start asking the university what it plans for nursing courses. I'd go to talks and write to the student paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be qualified and working before the robots arrive in 2034. That feels like both luck and a trap, because I'd be new in a job that machines are about to change. I'd rather not think about it too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work as a nurse for a couple of years, and learn on the job what the new tools do. I'd stay in the union and make sure the nursing contract keeps its protections. I'd also tell my younger cousin not to pick a desk-job degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mixed with a bit of dread. Five years is long enough to relax and short enough to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years feel safer or worse than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, because I'd have a full degree and some years of real work before the robots arrive. But it's worse than ten, because I'd still be early in my career when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you act differently if you knew for sure it was five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be more political. I'd join a campaign for retraining funds for nurses, since I wouldn't want the choice to be leave or be left behind.

say: We'd have some **warning**, so we should ask the university what it plans.
I'd go to talks and write for the **student paper**.
think: I'd be qualified before **2034**, which feels like luck and a trap.
I'd be new in a job that **machines** will change.
do: Finish the degree and work **two years** as a nurse first.
Stay in the union and protect **contract rights**.
Tell my younger cousin to avoid **desk-job degrees**.
feel: **Uneasy**, with some dread about being early in a changing job.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to relax and short enough to worry.
fieldNote: Five years lets her imagine a **working life** before the robots.
She picks **politics and union work** as her main response.
She is giving advice to relatives, which shows a protective streak.

steps.text: Finish the nursing degree and work two years on a ward
Campaign with the union for paid retraining for nurses
Write to the student paper about nursing and AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the best version, because there's time to make rules. I'd tell friends that ten years is enough for governments to protect nurses if people push. I'd keep voting and keep asking for decent funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel fairly calm for the bedside, but I'd still worry about everyone I know in office jobs. My dad's depot has a manager who does the schedules by hand, and I could see that being the first thing software replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take a ward job, and take the time to learn whichever tools come in, step by step. I'd pay into my pension from the start, and keep money aside in case I want to retrain as a midwife or health visitor later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. Not happy, but settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra time make you more or less active politically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More active, I think, because ten years is enough time to actually win something. I'd run a petition in my own hospital and try to get a ward representative role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own children to study, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with people in it. Healthcare, teaching, anything where somebody in the room needs a hand held. I don't think I'd tell them to avoid computers, just not to bet everything on them.

say: Ten years is **enough time** for rules, if people push.
I'd keep **voting** and asking for decent funding.
think: The bedside feels safe, but my **dad's depot** schedules could go to software.
I'd still worry about friends in **office jobs**.
do: Finish the degree, take a **ward job** and learn tools step by step.
Keep savings for retraining as a **midwife** if needed.
S4.quote: Something with people in it. Healthcare, teaching, anything where somebody in the room needs a hand held.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her activism from **fear to goals**.
She is worried about **other people** more than herself.
Her views on children's careers echo her own choice.

steps.text: Finish the nursing degree and start on a ward
Run a petition for nurse funding at the hospital
Open a pension contribution with the first nursing salary
Join the hospital ward representative group

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture, AGI by 2028, worries me most, because it leaves no room. If it happened, what would help is a clear promise from government that hospitals keep their nurses, plus paid training so we're not paying for it ourselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'm not against technology. I'm against nobody asking the people who actually look after patients. I'd like someone to ask ordinary students and nurses what we want before they roll it out.

headlineQuote: I'm not against technology. I'm against nobody asking the people who actually look after patients.
portrait: Aisha is a nursing student who **handwrites** her notes and avoids AI tools.
She is progressive, pro-union and blames **cuts and low taxes**, not the technology.
Her family pays everything, so money is calm and her worry is **timing**.
She feels safest with a ten-year warning and most frightened by **two years**.
Her instinct is to organise, petition and stay put on her course.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it leaves **no room** to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A government promise to protect **nurses' jobs** and pay for training.
